claim: Imaging data are typically collected during a behavioral task and stored for later offline analysis.
source: Imaging data are typically collected during a behavioral task and stored for later offline analysis, but emerging techniques for online imaging can support novel closed-loop experiments in which neural population activity is decoded in real time to trigger neurostimulation or sensory feedback.
evidence: This describes the typical workflow in calcium imaging experiments, which is established practice in the field.

evidence: This is a primary experimental result reported in the manuscript with data from 12 rats.

source: Miniature epifluorescence microscopes ('miniscopes') can be worn on the head of an unrestrained animal to perform in vivo calcium imaging of neural population activity during free behavior (Ghosh et al., 2011; Ziv et al., 2013; Cai et al., 2016; Aharoni et al., 2019; Hart et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Popular offline analysis packages such as CaImAn and MIN1PIPE employ algorithms for demixing crossover fluorescence between multiple sources to extract calcium traces from single neurons.
source: Popular offline analysis packages such as CaImAn (Giovannucci et al., 2019) and MIN1PIPE (Deng et al., 2015) employ algorithms (Pnevmatikakis et al., 2016) for demixing crossover fluorescence between multiple sources to extract calcium traces from single neurons, but these algorithms cannot be implemented in real time because they incur significant computing delays and rely on acausal computations.
evidence: This statement describes existing software tools and is supported by citations.

claim: CaImAn and MIN1PIPE algorithms cannot be implemented in real time because they incur significant computing delays and rely on acausal computations.
source: Popular offline analysis packages such as CaImAn (Giovannucci et al., 2019) and MIN1PIPE (Deng et al., 2015) employ algorithms (Pnevmatikakis et al., 2016) for demixing crossover fluorescence between multiple sources to extract calcium traces from single neurons, but these algorithms cannot be implemented in real time because they incur significant computing delays and rely on acausal computations.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of existing algorithms based on their computational characteristics.

claim: Emerging techniques for online trace extraction offer potential for carrying out real-time imaging experiments in which closed-loop neurostimulation or sensory feedback are triggered at short latencies in response to neural activity decoded from calcium fluorescence.

claim: Incoming frames arriving to the Ultra96 from the Miniscope DAQ are cropped to a 512 × 512 subregion, manually selected to contain the richest area of fluorescing neurons in each animal.

claim: A 128 × 128 pixel area with distinct anatomical features is manually selected during Stage 1 from within the 512 × 512 imaging subwindow to serve as a motion stabilization window.
source: To correct for translational movement of brain tissue, a 128 × 128 pixel area with distinct anatomical features is manually selected during Stage 1 (Figure 1B) from within the 512 × 512 imaging subwindow to serve as a motion stabilization window.
evidence: This describes the motion correction method with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: ACTEV's image stabilization algorithm rigidly corrects for translational movement of brain tissue by convolving the 128 × 128 stabilization window in each frame with a 17 × 17 contrast filter kernel.
source: ACTEV's image stabilization algorithm (Chen et al., 2019) rigidly corrects for translational movement of brain tissue by convolving the 128 × 128 stabilization window in each frame with a 17 × 17 contrast filter kernel, and then applying a fast 2D FFT/IFFT-based algorithm to correlate the stabilization window contents with a stored reference template (derived by averaging 1000 contrast-filtered frames from the beginning of each experimental session) to obtain a 2D motion displacement vector for the current frame.
evidence: This describes the motion correction algorithm, supported by a citation.

claim: After motion stabilization, ACTEV removes background fluorescence from the 512 × 512 image by performing a sequence of three enhancement operations: smoothing via convolution with a 3 × 3 mean filtering kernel, estimating the frame background via erosion and dilation with a 19 × 19 structuring element, and subtracting the estimated background from the smoothed image.
source: After motion stabilization, ACTEV removes background fluorescence from the 512 × 512 image by performing a sequence of three enhancement operations (Chen et al., 2020): smoothing via convolution with a 3 × 3 mean filtering kernel, estimating the frame background via erosion and dilation with a 19 × 19 structuring element (Lu et al., 2018), and subtracting the estimated background from the smoothed image.
evidence: This describes the background removal algorithm, supported by citations.

claim: To derive calcium trace values, the enhanced image is filtered through a library of up to 1024 binary pixel masks, each of which defines a unique ROI for extracting a calcium trace.
source: To derive calcium trace values, the enhanced image is filtered through a library of up to 1024 binary pixel masks, each of which defines a unique ROI for extracting a calcium trace.
evidence: This describes the trace extraction method.

claim: Each mask is defined as a selected subset of pixels within a 25 × 25 square region that can be centered anywhere in the 512 × 512 imaging subwindow.
source: Each mask is defined as a selected subset of pixels within a 25 × 25 square region that can be centered anywhere in the 512 × 512 imaging subwindow (Figure 2, upper left).
evidence: This describes the ROI mask specifications with reference to Figure 2.

evidence: This describes the contour-based method, supported by a citation.

claim: For contour-free ROI selection, the 512 × 512 imaging subwindow pixel was uniformly covered with a 32 × 32 array of square tiles, each measuring 16 × 16 pixels, which served as ROIs for calcium trace extraction.
source: For contour-free ROI selection, the 512 × 512 imaging subwindow pixel was uniformly covered with a 32 × 32 array of square tiles, each measuring 16 × 16 pixels, which served as ROIs for calcium trace extraction.

source: This contour-free approach did not align ROIs with individual neurons, so each extracted calcium trace could detect fluorescence originating from more than one neuron.

source: For real-time decoding, we did not define a decision boundary for classifying CA1 traces as coming from 'place' versus 'non-place' cells; calcium traces were decoded from all ROIs regardless of their spatial tuning properties.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice in the decoding approach.

claim: Speed filtering was not implemented during online decoding of CA1 fluorescence because the linear classifier received only real-time calcium trace data and not position tracking data that would be needed for speed filtering.
source: Here, speed filtering was not implemented during online decoding of CA1 fluorescence because the linear classifier received only real-time calcium trace data and not position tracking data that would be needed for speed filtering.
evidence: This explains a methodological limitation and design choice.

claim: DeCalciOn achieved accurate decoding of the rat's position from calcium traces without speed filtering.
source: As shown below, DeCalciOn achieved accurate decoding of the rat's position from calcium traces without speed filtering.
evidence: This is a finding demonstrated in the manuscript's experiments.

claim: The GCamp7s indicator used in CA1 imaging experiments has a decay constant of several hundred ms.
source: The GCamp7s indicator used in our CA1 imaging experiments has a decay constant of several hundred ms (Dana et al., 2019), which is similar to the width of time bins typically used for counting spikes when decoding a rat's position from single-unit recordings of place cells (Ziv et al., 2013; Cai et al., 2016; Wilson and McNaughton, 1993; Kinsky et al., 2018; Center for Brains Minds Machines, 2017).
evidence: This is a property of the calcium indicator, supported by a citation.

claim: The linear classifier was more accurate at decoding the rat's position from raw calcium trace amplitudes than from inferred spike counts.
source: In accordance with prior studies of position decoding from CA1 calcium fluorescence (Tu et al., 2020), we found (see panel A of Supplement to Figure 3) that the linear classifier was more accurate at decoding the rat's position from raw calcium trace amplitudes (which chemically time-integrated spikes on a time scale of the several hundred milliseconds, corresponding to the GCaMP7s decay rate) than from inferred spike counts (which computationally time-integrated spike counts on a much shorter time scale of ~50 ms, corresponding to the miniscope's frame interval).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with reference to supplementary data, supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The linear classifier was trained on calcium trace and position data from the first half of each session, then tested on data from the second half of the session.
source: The linear classifier was trained on calcium trace and position data from the first half of each session, then tested on data from the second half of the session.
evidence: This describes the training and testing protocol.

claim: The classifier's output vector consisted of 12 units that used a Gray coding scheme to represent 24 position bins along a circularized representation of the track.
source: The classifier's output vector consisted of 12 units that used a Gray coding scheme (Figure 3B) to represent 24 position bins (each ~20 cm wide) along a circularized representation of the track.
evidence: This describes the decoder architecture with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: Running CaImAn on 4K–5K frames of training data required 30–60 min of computing time on the host PC.
source: Running CaImAn on 4K–5K frames of training data required 30–60 min of computing time on the host PC, making this the slowest step performed during the intermission period (see Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a timing measurement from the experimental protocol.

claim: After contour ROIs had been identified, an additional ~5 min of computing time was required to feed all of the training data frames through a simulator to reconstruct online calcium traces.
source: After contour ROIs had been identified, an additional ~5 min of computing time was required to feed all of the training data frames through a simulator to reconstruct online calcium traces that would have been extracted in real time during the first half of the session using the extracted contour masks.
evidence: This is a timing measurement from the experimental protocol.

claim: Training the decoder required a maximum ~60 s of computing time.
source: The simulated online traces were then aligned frame-by-frame with position data and used to train a linear classifier for decoding the rat's position on the linear track from calcium activity; training the decoder required a maximum ~60 s of computing time.
evidence: This is a timing measurement from the experimental protocol.

claim: Large proportions of CB traces in CA1 exhibited stable spatial tuning between the training and testing epochs, as required for accurate decoding.
source: Analyses of spatial selectivity and within-session spatial tuning stability (panels D, E in Supplement to Figure 3) indicated that large proportions of CB traces in CA1 exhibited stable spatial tuning between the training and testing epochs, as required for accurate decoding.
evidence: This is an analysis result with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: The real-time decoder was trained and tested on CB traces from all ROIs identified by CaImAn in each session.
source: The real-time decoder was trained and tested on CB traces from all ROIs identified by CaImAn in each session; we did not restrict the decoder's training set to a subset of traces that met a spatial selectivity criterion.
evidence: This describes the training methodology.

claim: CF extraction always yielded a total of 900 calcium traces per rat (one for each square tile).
source: The CF extraction method always yielded a total of 900 calcium traces per rat (one for each square tile).
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the contour-free method.

claim: The CB method yielded a variable number of traces depending upon how many neuron ROIs were detected in the training dataset by CaImAn.
source: By contrast, the CB method (see above) yielded a variable number of traces depending upon how many neuron ROIs were detected in the training dataset by CaImAn.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the contour-based method.

claim: CF trace extraction does not require any computing time for contour identification or trace simulation during the intermission period.
source: Unlike CB trace extraction, CF extraction does not require any computing time for contour identification or trace simulation during the intermission period, because the decoder is trained directly on 900 traces of CF data stored to memory during the training epoch; this training consumed <60 s of computing time on the host PC for 5K frames of training data.
evidence: This describes an efficiency advantage of the contour-free method.

claim: CF traces in CA1 exhibited stable spatially selective tuning.
source: Like CB traces, CF traces in CA1 also exhibited stable spatially selective tuning (Figure 3D, middle).
evidence: This is an experimental observation with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: Individual CF traces showed less within-session stability and fired over wider regions of the track than individual CB traces.
source: However, individual CF traces showed less within-session stability and fired over wider regions of the track (panels D, E in Supplement to Figure 3) than individual CB traces, as should be expected if CF traces contain signals from multiple place cells and CB traces isolate signals from individual place cells.
evidence: This is an experimental observation with reference to supplementary figures, along with an inference about the cause.

claim: At the population level, decoding the rat's position from CF traces was as or more accurate than decoding from CB traces.
source: But at the population level, decoding the rat's position from CF traces was as or more accurate than decoding from CB traces.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental results.

claim: Decoding from multiunit spike trains can be more accurate than decoding from sorted spikes sourced to single units.
source: Analogous results have been reported in electrophysiology, where it has been found that decoding from multiunit spike trains can be more accurate than decoding from sorted spikes sourced to single units (Deng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work in electrophysiology, supported by a citation.

claim: CF and CB+ traces yielded similar decoding accuracy, suggesting that the number of calcium trace predictors was a strong determinant of decoding accuracy.
source: Hence, CF and CB+ traces yielded similar decoding accuracy, suggesting that the number of calcium trace predictors was a strong determinant of decoding accuracy.

source: Deriving CB+ traces required about the same amount of computing time (30–60 min) during the intermission period as CB traces to identify contours and simulate online traces (see Figure 1B). Therefore, despite the similar accuracy of CF and CB+ traces, it was much more efficient to use CF traces since they did not require extra computing time to identify ROIs during the intermission period.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the computational efficiency of the two methods.

claim: On average, asymptotic accuracy occurred when the training epoch reached ~3000 frames, beyond which increasing the duration of the training epoch yielded diminishing benefits for decoding accuracy.

evidence: This is a statement about computational resource usage, supported by a citation.

claim: Online motion stabilization was effective at correcting shift errors in the one session where they occurred.
source: Hence, online motion stabilization was effective at correcting shift errors in the one session where they occurred; but given that shift errors occurred so rarely, it might be argued that correcting these errors does not adequately justify resource costs of online motion stabilization, especially if shift errors can be effectively prevented by other means such as rigidly attaching the miniscope to the baseplate.

source: Jitter error occurs when the animal's inertial head acceleration causes transient motion of the brain inside the skull cavity, resulting in phasic translation of the brain image across the sensor.

source: Motion of the brain inside the skull is a natural phenomenon during free behavior, and for this reason, jitter error cannot easily be prevented by means other than online motion stabilization.
evidence: This is a statement about a biological phenomenon and its implications.

evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

Sensitivity for detecting reward retrieval was higher for Rat JL66 than JL63, which is not surprising since predictions were derived from a larger number of detected neurons in Rat JL66.

source: The F-score was higher for CF than Off or CB traces in Rat JL63 but not JL66, suggesting that in cases where a small number of neurons are detected (as in Rat JL63), decoder precision can be improved by using CF rather than CB traces.

source: In both rats, real-time decoding of reward retrieval and correct choice events was similarly accurate (from both CB and CF traces) regardless of whether online motion correction was used (mc+ vs. mc−; Figure 5D–F).

source: To put this feedback latency into the context of the rat's behavior, a freely behaving rat can travel ~7.5 cm in 47.5 ms if it is running at the maximum observed speed on the linear track of ~150 cm/s (see panel A in Supplement to Figure 3).
evidence: This is a calculated value based on observed running speeds.

claim: When a maximum likelihood decoder is used to predict a rat's position on a linear track from single-unit spike trains of 53 place cells at a 47.5-ms latency from the rat's true position, the distance error asymptotes at a minimum of ~20 cm for spike count time windows longer than ~0.5 s.
source: Figure 7E shows that when a maximum likelihood decoder is used to predict a rat's position on a linear track from single-unit spike trains of 53 place cells (Center for Brains Minds Machines, 2017) at a 47.5-ms latency from the rat's true position, the distance error asymptotes at a minimum of ~20 cm for spike count time windows longer than ~0.5 s.

claim: Real-time decoding of calcium traces with DeCalciOn achieves distance errors that are within a similar range as those seen in offline analysis of place cell spike trains.
source: Hence, real-time decoding of calcium traces with DeCalciOn achieves distance errors that are within a similar range as those seen in offline analysis of place cell spike trains.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the performance of calcium imaging versus single-unit recordings.

claim: Most in vivo calcium imaging experiments utilize offline algorithms to analyze calcium trace data that has previously been collected and stored during a behavioral task.
source: Most in vivo calcium imaging experiments utilize offline algorithms to analyze calcium trace data that has previously been collected and stored during a behavioral task.
evidence: This is a statement about common practice in the field.

claim: Accurate source identification is important for studies where investigating the tuning properties of individual neurons is a major aim of data analysis.
source: Accurate source identification is important for studies where investigating the tuning properties of individual neurons is a major aim of data analysis, but DeCalciOn is designed for real-time imaging experiments in which fast and accurate decoding of behavior from neural population activity takes precedence over characterizing single-neuron firing properties.
evidence: This is a statement about the design priorities of DeCalciOn.

claim: For real-time decoding, the high computational costs of source identification may not yield proportional benefits to decoding accuracy.
source: For real-time decoding, the high computational costs of source identification may not yield proportional benefits to decoding accuracy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Linear classifiers trained on calcium traces extracted online (without demixing) predicted behavior just as accurately as those trained on traces extracted offline (with demixing) using the same set of ROIs.
source: Supporting this, we found that linear classifiers trained on calcium traces extracted online (without demixing) predicted behavior just as accurately as those trained on traces extracted offline (with demixing) using the same set of ROIs (Figure 3E; Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with references to figures.

claim: Decoders trained on traces extracted from contour-free ROIs predicted behavior as or more accurately than traces extracted from contour-based ROIs that overlapped with identified neurons in the image frame.
source: We also found that decoders trained on traces extracted from contour-free ROIs (which do not overlap with individual neurons) predicted behavior as or more accurately than traces extracted from contour-based ROIs that overlapped with identified neurons in the image frame (Figure 3F and G; Figure 4A and B; Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with references to multiple figures.

claim: In electrophysiology studies, 'spike sorting' algorithms for sourcing action potentials to single neurons incur high computational overhead costs that are comparable to the costs of sourcing calcium traces to single neurons with CNMF.
source: Analogous results have been reported in electrophysiology, where 'spike sorting' algorithms for sourcing action potentials to single neurons incur high computational overhead costs that are comparable to the costs of sourcing calcium traces to single neurons with CNMF; decoding behavior from electrophysiological recordings of multiunit (unsorted) spikes is more computationally efficient than decoding from sorted spikes and often incurs no cost (or even a benefit) to decoding accuracy (Deng et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work in electrophysiology, supported by a citation.

claim: For real-time imaging studies, contour-free decoding approaches can offer a strategy for optimizing computing efficiency without compromising decoding accuracy.
source: Results presented here indicate that as in electrophysiology studies, the high computing cost of source identification in calcium imaging studies must be weighed against the benefits. For real-time imaging studies, contour-free decoding approaches can offer a strategy for optimizing computing efficiency without compromising decoding accuracy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: After source identification, the most computationally expensive stage in the image processing pipeline is motion stabilization.
source: After source identification, the most computationally expensive stage in the image processing pipeline is motion stabilization.
evidence: This is a statement about computational resource usage.

claim: Online motion correction prevented decoding accuracy from becoming degraded during frames in which brain motion shifted the sensor image.
source: We found that online motion stabilization was effective at preventing two problems that can arise from instability of the brain image on the sensor. First, when decoding a rat's position on the linear track, online motion correction prevented decoding accuracy from becoming degraded during frames in which brain motion shifted the sensor image, as evidenced by the fact the positive correlations between decoding error and image displacement were reduced by online motion correction (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with reference to Figure 4.

claim: In the instrumental touch screen task where brain motion was significantly correlated with specific behaviors, the decoder learned to predict behavior from image motion (rather than calcium fluorescence) in the absence of motion correction.
source: Second, in the instrumental touch screen task where brain motion was significantly correlated with specific behaviors, the decoder learned to predict behavior from image motion (rather than calcium fluorescence) in the absence of motion correction; the decoder was prevented from learning these ersatz predictions when the online motion correction algorithm was applied to the decoder's training and testing datasets (Figure 5D–F; Figure 6).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with references to figures.

claim: For real-time feedback experiments, the session-averaged prediction accuracy is not the most important measure of decoder performance.
source: However, for real-time feedback experiments, the session-averaged prediction accuracy is not the most important measure of decoder performance. What matters most is the accuracy of decoding during specific frames when it is important for feedback stimulation to be delivered or withheld.
evidence: This is a statement about the appropriate performance metric for real-time systems.

claim: If frames requiring accurate feedback happen to overlap with motion artifact that interferes with decoding accuracy, then failure to perform motion correction can have disastrous consequences for feedback experiments, regardless of whether or not motion correction improves the 'average' decoding accuracy.
source: If such frames happen to overlap with motion artifact that interferes with decoding accuracy, then failure to perform motion correction can have disastrous consequences for feedback experiments, regardless of whether or not motion correction improves the 'average' decoding accuracy.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the importance of motion correction for specific frames.

claim: The high resource costs of online motion correction are well worth the benefits they accrue by increasing the reliability of online decoding of neural population activity.
source: Based on these considerations and the results of our performance tests, we conclude that the high resource costs of online motion correction are well worth the benefits they accrue by increasing the reliability of online decoding of neural population activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results and considerations.

source: Liu et al., 2021 showed that their system can implement a single binary classifier to decode calcium traces from 10 ROIs in mouse cortex at latencies <3 ms; this latency measurement appears to only include the decoder's execution time for generating predictions from calcium vectors (equivalent to Step 4 of our image processing pipeline) but not the light-gathering delay time (Figure 7A) or data buffering time.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work, supported by a citation, with an interpretation of what the latency measurement includes.

source: Zhang et al., 2018 performed 2-photon calcium imaging experiments that incorporated real-time image processing on a GPU to detect neural activity and trigger closed-loop optical feedback stimulation in mouse cortex.

source: Summing this latency with the light-gathering delay (~15 ms at the system's default 30-Hz frame rate), data buffering delay (reported to be ~2.5 ms), online motion correction delay (reported to be ~3.5 ms), and decoder execution time (~2 ms), it can be estimated that when decoding 1024 traces, Zhang et al., 2018 system would incur a delay of ~75 ms between light arriving at the sensor and triggering of closed-loop feedback.
evidence: This is a calculated estimate based on reported values from the cited work.

source: This latency is only 25 ms (~50%) longer than DeCalciOn's 47.5-ms decoding latency under similar conditions (Figure 7), and could possibly be improved using parallelization or other efficiency strategies.

source: Although latency performance is similar for DeCalciOn's FPGA-based pipeline and Zhang et al., 2018 GPU-based pipeline, the two systems have different hardware compatibilities: DeCalciOn is designed for compatibility with head-free miniscopes that use the UCLA DAQ interface, whereas Zhang et al., 2018 system is designed for compatibility with hardware and software interface standards used in benchtop multiphoton imaging systems.

claim: At the end of the experiment, rats were anesthetized with isoflurane, intraperitoneally injected with 1 ml of pentobarbital, then transcardially perfused with 100 ml of 0.01 M phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) followed by 200 ml of 4% paraformaldehyde in 0.01 M PBS to fix the brain tissue.
source: At the end of the experiment, rats were anesthetized with isoflurane, intraperitoneally injected with 1 ml of pentobarbital, then transcardially perfused with 100 ml of 0.01 M phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) followed by 200 ml of 4% paraformaldehyde in 0.01 M PBS to fix the brain tissue.
evidence: This describes the histology procedure.

claim: Brains were sectioned at 40-µm thickness on a cryostat, mounted on gelatin prepared slides, then imaged on a confocal microscope to confirm GFP expression and GRIN lens placement.
source: Brains were sectioned at 40-µm thickness on a cryostat (Leica), mounted on gelatin prepared slides, then imaged on a confocal microscope (Zeiss) to confirm GFP expression and GRIN lens placement.
evidence: This describes the histological verification procedure.

claim: The DeCalciOn system is designed for use with UCLA Miniscope devices and other miniscopes that use the UCLA DAQ interface.
source: The DeCalciOn system is designed for use with UCLA Miniscope devices (Cai et al., 2016) and other miniscopes (Scott et al., 2018; de Groot et al., 2020; Blair et al., 2021) that use the UCLA DAQ interface.
evidence: This describes the hardware compatibility of DeCalciOn, supported by citations.

claim: The DAQ hardware requires modification by soldering flywires to the PCB.
source: The DAQ hardware requires modification by soldering flywires to the PCB (see Figure 1); instructions for doing this are available at https://github.com/zhe-ch/ACTEV (Chen, 2023 copy archived at swh:1:rev:aa6393d3bd2dd490aa5369e1f2677e85e8a64a82) and pre-modified DAQ boards are available at miniscope.org.
evidence: This describes a hardware modification requirement.

claim: DeCalciOn is implemented on an Avnet Ultra96 development board.
source: DeCalciOn is implemented on an Avnet Ultra96 development board (available from the manufacturer at Avnet.com), which must be mated to our custom interface board available at miniscope.org (the interface can also be ordered from a PCB manufacturer with design files available at https://github.com/zhe-ch/ACTEV) (Chen, 2023 copy archived at swh:1:rev:aa6393d3bd2dd490aa5369e1f2677e85e8a64a82).
evidence: This describes the hardware platform and availability.

claim: Real-time imaging and decoding are controlled by custom RTI software which runs on the host PC alongside standard DAQ software.
source: Real-time imaging and decoding are controlled by custom RTI software (available at https://github.com/zhe-ch/ACTEV) (Chen, 2023 copy archived at swh:1:rev:aa6393d3bd2dd490aa5369e1f2677e85e8a64a82) which runs on the host PC alongside standard DAQ software (available at miniscope.org) for adjusting the gain and focus of the Miniscope device.
evidence: This describes the software control system.

claim: Pixel masks for contour-based trace extraction were derived using the CaImAn pipeline to analyze motion-corrected sensor images from the training dataset.
source: Pixel masks for contour-based trace extraction were derived using the CaImAn (Giovannucci et al., 2019) pipeline (implemented in python) to analyze motion-corrected sensor images from the training dataset (as noted in the main text, this took 30–60 min of computing time on the host PC).
evidence: This describes the method for deriving contour-based pixel masks, supported by a citation.

claim: To implement contour-free trace extraction, the 512 × 512 image frame was partitioned into a 32 × 32 sheet of tiles, each measuring a square of 16 × 16 pixels.
source: To implement contour-free trace extraction, we simply partitioned the 512 × 512 image frame into a 32 × 32 sheet of tiles, each measuring a square of 16 × 16 pixels (Figure 4B).
evidence: This describes the contour-free method with reference to a figure.

claim: No traces were extracted from 124 tiles bordering the edge of the frame, to avoid noise artifacts that might arise from edge effects in the motion stabilization algorithm.
source: No traces were extracted from 124 tiles bordering the edge of the frame, to avoid noise artifacts that might arise from edge effects in the motion stabilization algorithm.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice to avoid artifacts.

claim: A total of 900 pixel mask tiles were used for contour-free calcium trace extraction.
source: Hence, a total of 1024–124 = 900 pixel mask tiles were used for contour-free calcium trace extraction.
evidence: This is a calculated value based on the tile arrangement.

claim: An advantage of contour-free trace extraction is that the intermission period between training and testing is shortened to just a few minutes, because the lengthy process of contour identification is no longer required.
source: These traces were derived in real time and stored to the host PC throughout the initial data acquisition period, so they were immediately available for training the linear classifier at the start of the intermission. Consequently, an advantage of contour-free trace extraction is that the intermission period between training and testing is shortened to just a few minutes, because the lengthy process of contour identification is no longer required.
evidence: This describes an efficiency advantage of the contour-free method.

claim: A disadvantage of contour-free trace extraction is that contour tiles do not align with individual neurons in the sensor image.
source: A disadvantage of contour-free trace extraction is that contour tiles do not align with individual neurons in the sensor image.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the contour-free method.

claim: Contour-free decoding places limits upon what can be inferred about how single neurons represent information in imaged brain regions.
source: As reported in the main text, this lack of alignment between neurons and pixel masks did not impair (and often enhanced) position decoding; however, contour-free decoding does place limits upon what can be inferred about how single neurons represent information in imaged brain regions.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of the contour-free method for neuroscience interpretation.
